newsitem.title: UK: UK lobby group counts cost of scapping duty free.
newsitem.headline: UK lobby group counts cost of scapping duty free.

text.p: The British duty free industry on Wednesday stepped up its campaign to preserve duty and tax free shopping in the European Union, saying its planned abolition would hit key industries and government finances.

An independent study commissioned by lobby group the Duty Free Confederation showed that instead of boosting government coffers, scrapping duty free could cut Britain's state revenues by 18 million pounds ($28.6 million) a year.

Spokesman Barry Goddard said the report, prepared by National Economic Research Associates, dispelled the myth that public finances would be boosted if duty free -- with four billion pounds annual turnover in the EU -- were abolished as planned on June 30, 1999.
Goddard said the duty free issue was not only important to Britain and there was widespread support for the cause across the European Union.
"We have enthusiastic support in the EU," he told a news conference.

He said Spain and Greece were worried abolition would make charter travel more expensive and divert tourists to cheaper destinations outside the EU. France was concerned about the impact on its luxury goods industries.

The study calculated that the government would receive about 120 million pounds from duty and VAT receipts if duty free were to go. But this would be offset by a 114 million pound drop in corporation tax payments from firms whose profits would suffer.

The report estimated retailers profits could fall by as much as 280 million pounds a year, and manufacturers by 65 million. Around 1,500 jobs could go, which would represent a net cost to the government of 21 million pounds.

Without duty free, the levels of sales at British duty and tax free retail outlets - airports, airlines and ferries - would decline sharply. A large proportion of the expenditure would switch to duty paid goods in continental Europe, where the level of duty is often much lower than in Britain. The report found that 90 percent of travel from Britain was to countries with lower taxes in liquor and tobacco.

Sarah Branquinho, who heads the European Travel Research Foundation, said other studies were looking into the impact on travel costs, including a ferry sector survey which showed some routes could be at risk if duty free sales were scrapped.

Goddard said his organisation and others across the EU would lobby national governments and MEPs on the issue. He was optimistic the European Parliament would support them and ask the European Commission to look again at the abolition plans. -- Jane Merriman, London Newsroom + 44 171 542 7717 ($ = 0.629 British Pounds)
